def: Reproductive cells produced by fungi, such as conidia (asexual spores borne on hyphae). Inhaled conidia of molds like Aspergillus can start infection in the lungs.
The compartment between the inner and outer membranes of gram-negative bacteria. It holds peptidoglycan and beta-lactamases and is absent in gram-positive bacteria.
Steroid-based lipids with a hydroxyl group on a four-ring structure. Cholesterol is the main animal sterol and ergosterol the main fungal sterol.
A walled-off collection of pus within the abdominal cavity, often after surgery, perforation or diverticulitis. It causes fever and pain and usually needs drainage plus antibiotics.
A body-wide inflammatory state with abnormal temperature, heart rate, respiratory rate and white cell count. It may be triggered by infection, burns or pancreatitis; with infection it defines sepsis.
A bacteriophage life cycle in which viral DNA integrates into the bacterial chromosome as a prophage and replicates silently with the host, rather than killing it at once.
Cholesterol carried by high-density lipoprotein, which moves cholesterol from tissues back to the liver. High levels are protective against atherosclerosis.
Blood glucose above normal but below diabetes thresholds (fasting glucose 100-125 mg/dL, HbA1c 5.7-6.4%), reflecting insulin resistance and raising later diabetes risk.
The complete nucleic acid of a virus, which may be DNA or RNA, single- or double-stranded, and is packaged inside the capsid.
An oral alpha-1 agonist that constricts vessels to raise blood pressure, used for orthostatic hypotension. It can cause supine hypertension.
An isotonic IV fluid containing sodium, potassium, calcium, chloride and lactate. The lactate is metabolized to bicarbonate, making it useful for resuscitation and burns.
Fluids with the same osmolarity as plasma, so they do not shift water across cell membranes. Normal saline (0.9% NaCl) is the classic example.
A common benign firm skin nodule, usually on the legs of adults, made of fibroblasts. It dimples inward when pinched.
A bacterial toxin that lyses red blood cells by forming pores in their membranes. Examples include streptolysin O and staphylococcal alpha toxin.
A viridans group streptococcus normally found in the mouth that can enter the blood after dental procedures and cause subacute bacterial endocarditis on damaged valves.
A lipophilic antimycobacterial drug used for leprosy (Hansen disease) and drug-resistant mycobacterial infections. It causes reddish-brown skin discoloration.
Abnormally large, immature red cell precursors with open nuclear chromatin due to impaired DNA synthesis, seen in vitamin B12 and folate deficiency.
An oral third-generation cephalosporin used for respiratory, urinary and skin infections.
Hepatitis B infection persisting longer than 6 months (HBsAg positive). It can lead to cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma and is treated with antivirals such as entecavir and tenofovir.
A chronic suppurative infection by anaerobic filamentous gram-positive bacteria, usually Actinomyces israelii, forming abscesses and draining sinuses with sulfur granules, often in the jaw.
An HIV integrase strand transfer inhibitor that blocks insertion of viral DNA into the host genome.
An integrase strand transfer inhibitor used in HIV combination therapy. It can raise serum creatinine by blocking tubular secretion.
Infections within the peritoneal cavity or abdominal organs, such as peritonitis, appendicitis, diverticulitis and abscesses, usually mixed enteric flora.
A plot of a test's sensitivity against its false positive rate (1 minus specificity) at varying cutoffs. The area under the curve measures overall diagnostic accuracy.
Compounds made of a lipid attached to a peptide. The antibiotic daptomycin is a lipopeptide that depolarizes gram-positive cell membranes.
The large RNA component of the bacterial 50S ribosomal subunit. Macrolides, clindamycin, linezolid and streptogramins bind it; methylation causes resistance.

Thickening of the pyloric muscle in infants, usually weeks after birth, causing projectile nonbilious vomiting and an olive-shaped abdominal mass. It causes hypochloremic hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis.
Infection of the lacrimal sac, usually from nasolacrimal duct obstruction, causing painful swelling below the medial corner of the eye.
The channel that drains tears from the lacrimal sac into the nose beneath the inferior turbinate. Failure to open at birth causes tearing and eye discharge.
Blockage of tear drainage, often congenital in infants from an imperforate membrane at the duct's end, or acquired in adults. It leads to tearing and recurrent infection.
An antihistamine and mast cell stabilizer eye drop used for allergic conjunctivitis.
Washing out the stomach through a tube, once used for poisonings and overdoses. It is rarely done now because of aspiration risk.
Antibiotics such as quinupristin-dalfopristin that bind the 50S ribosome, used for vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus faecium.
An aminoglycoside antibiotic with good activity against Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Toxicities are nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity.
Inhibitory interneurons in the ventral spinal cord that receive collaterals from alpha motor neurons and inhibit them via glycine. Tetanus toxin blocks their release of glycine.
The integrated bacteriophage DNA within a bacterial chromosome during lysogeny. It can carry toxin genes, such as diphtheria and cholera toxin.
G protein-coupled receptors that bind chemokines to direct leukocyte migration. CCR5 is a co-receptor for HIV entry.
The expanding red ring rash of early Lyme disease at the site of an Ixodes tick bite, often with central clearing.
Nerve pain persisting for months after a herpes zoster (shingles) outbreak in the same dermatome, treated with gabapentin, tricyclics or topical lidocaine.
A nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor for HIV. Patients carrying the HLA-B5701 allele are at risk of a severe hypersensitivity reaction.
A non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor for HIV-1, now rarely used.
An injected HIV fusion inhibitor that binds gp41 and blocks viral fusion with the host cell.
A mesenchymal tumor of the GI tract arising from interstitial cells of Cajal, usually in the stomach. It often has KIT or PDGFRA mutations and is treated with imatinib.
An enzyme that adds phosphate to serine or threonine residues of target proteins, regulating signaling. Examples include Raf, Akt and mTOR.
The protein product of the NF2 tumor suppressor gene (schwannomin). Its loss causes neurofibromatosis type 2, with bilateral vestibular schwannomas and meningiomas.
A psychotherapy for post-traumatic stress disorder in which the patient recalls trauma while following bilateral eye movements.
The first fully formed purine nucleotide in de novo synthesis, the precursor of AMP and GMP.
A platinum alkylating-type chemotherapy drug that cross-links DNA. It is less nephrotoxic and neurotoxic than cisplatin but more myelosuppressive.
An iron-chelating agent that protects the heart from doxorubicin cardiotoxicity.
Repeated passage of stool into clothing in a child older than 4, usually from chronic constipation with overflow incontinence.
Proteins with attached carbohydrate chains embedded in membranes, serving in cell recognition, adhesion and as viral receptors.
The specialized epithelium of the upper nasal cavity containing olfactory receptor neurons, whose axons pass through the cribriform plate.
A sandfly-transmitted protozoal skin infection causing painless ulcers that heal with scarring. Amastigotes are found within macrophages.
A sandfly-borne protozoan that causes visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar), with fever, hepatosplenomegaly, pancytopenia and hyperpigmentation.
Fast-acting antimalarial drugs derived from sweet wormwood, such as artesunate, used for severe falciparum malaria.
Antimalarial drugs such as chloroquine, quinine and mefloquine that interfere with heme detoxification in Plasmodium.
A disease from the filarial worm Onchocerca volvulus, transmitted by blackflies. It causes itchy skin nodules and "river blindness"; treated with ivermectin.
An antifilarial drug used for lymphatic filariasis and loiasis.
The beef tapeworm, acquired by eating undercooked beef. It causes mild intestinal infection and does not cause cysticercosis.
Intestinal infection by adult tapeworms of the genus Taenia, from eating undercooked pork or beef.
A gram-negative rod causing severe bacillary dysentery; its Shiga toxin inhibits the 60S ribosomal subunit and can cause hemolytic uremic syndrome.
A diarrheagenic E. coli that attaches to enterocytes and effaces the brush border, causing watery diarrhea in infants.
Use of heat from electric current to seal bleeding vessels or destroy tissue.
Deposition of beta-amyloid in cerebral small vessel walls of older adults, causing lobar intracerebral hemorrhage and dementia. It is stained by Congo red with apple-green birefringence.
Imaging that uses strong magnetic fields and radio waves to image soft tissue without ionizing radiation.
A tear in the arterial intima that lets blood enter the wall and split its layers, as in aortic dissection or carotid dissection.
An organochlorine insecticide once used topically for scabies and lice; neurotoxic and seizure-inducing.
Tiny arthropods such as Sarcoptes scabiei, which cause scabies, and Demodex, which live in hair follicles.
A hip flexor muscle from the lumbar spine to the lesser trochanter. Psoas abscess or irritation causes pain with hip extension.
Blood flow between mother and fetus: maternal blood bathes the chorionic villi in the intervillous space while fetal blood flows in umbilical vessels.
Determination of ABO and Rh antigens on red cells; crossmatching tests donor cells against recipient serum to prevent transfusion reactions.
Hemolytic disease of the newborn from maternal IgG antibodies against fetal red cells, typically Rh incompatibility. It causes anemia, jaundice and hydrops.
Testing a person's human leukocyte antigen alleles to match donors and recipients in transplantation.
The cup-shaped socket of the pelvis (formed by ilium, ischium and pubis) that receives the femoral head.
The antibody class secreted at mucosal surfaces as a dimer with a J chain and secretory piece, protecting mucous membranes. It is present in breast milk.
The prototype of norovirus, a calicivirus causing outbreaks of acute viral gastroenteritis.
Narrowing of the main or branch pulmonary arteries, seen in Williams syndrome, congenital rubella and Alagille syndrome.
Glycoproteins embedded in a virus's lipid envelope that bind host receptors and mediate fusion, such as HIV gp120 and gp41.
The medial forearm bone; its trochlear notch articulates with the humerus at the elbow. Olecranon fracture is common.
A pattern of birth defects after fetal Zika infection, including microcephaly, brain calcifications, eye abnormalities and contractures.
A filovirus related to Ebola that causes severe hemorrhagic fever, spread through body fluids and linked to fruit bats.
A hantavirus disease (Hantaan, Seoul) causing fever, thrombocytopenia, hemorrhage and acute kidney injury.
A mosquito-borne bunyavirus disease of livestock and humans in Africa, causing fever, hepatitis, retinitis and hemorrhage.
A mosquito-borne bunyavirus (La Crosse) encephalitis affecting children in the US Midwest and Southeast.
A disseminated herpes simplex skin infection in patients with atopic dermatitis, with clustered punched-out vesicles.
A benign collection of melanocytes in the skin (a mole). Atypical features suggest melanoma.
Infection by a double-stranded segmented RNA reovirus, the leading cause of severe watery diarrhea in unvaccinated infants.
A break of the distal tibia or fibula. Lateral malleolus fractures are common and the Ottawa ankle rules guide imaging.
A B-cell lymphoma presenting as fluid in body cavities, caused by HHV-8 and seen in HIV patients.
Pharyngeal tonsils: lymphoid tissue on the roof of the nasopharynx. Enlargement obstructs nasal breathing and the eustachian tubes.
Inward misdirection of eyelashes that rub against the cornea. A major complication of trachoma.
Primary herpes simplex infection of the mouth in children, with painful vesicles and ulcers of the gingiva and oral mucosa.
A congenital foot deformity with plantar flexion, inversion and forefoot adduction (talipes equinovarus).
Forward slippage of one vertebra over the one below it, most often L5 on S1, causing low back pain. It results from spondylolysis (a pars interarticularis defect).
Ether phospholipids abundant in myelin and heart. Their synthesis begins in peroxisomes and is impaired in Zellweger syndrome.
A mitochondrial inherited cause of painless central vision loss in young men, from complex I mutations.
The most common lung cancer, usually peripheral, arising from glandular cells. It is common in nonsmokers and may carry EGFR or ALK mutations.
Intracellular proteins that link cadherins to the actin cytoskeleton. Beta-catenin also acts in Wnt signaling and is mutated in some tumors.
A developmental signaling pathway in which Wnt proteins stabilize beta-catenin to turn on target genes. APC mutation in colon cancer upregulates it.
A congenital absence of the pulmonary valve opening, blocking blood from the right ventricle to the lungs. Survival depends on a patent ductus arteriosus.
Vaginal bleeding in early pregnancy with a closed cervix and a viable fetus.
Fetal death in early pregnancy with a closed cervix and retained products, without bleeding or cramping.
Imaging that reconstructs cross-sectional images from many x-ray projections.
Infection by parvovirus B19, causing erythema infectiosum (fifth disease) with slapped-cheek rash, aplastic crisis in hemolytic anemia and hydrops fetalis.
Passage of fetal blood into the maternal circulation, which can sensitize an Rh-negative mother; RhoGAM prevents this.
An anticholinergic (antimuscarinic) drug used for GI spasm, bladder spasm and drooling.
Anticholinergic drugs that relax smooth muscle of the gut and bladder, such as dicyclomine and hyoscyamine.
Normal or excessive inward curvature of the lumbar spine.
Axons of sympathetic ganglion neurons that release norepinephrine on target organs. Sweat glands are an exception, using acetylcholine.
A gap in the eye structure (iris, retina or optic nerve) from failed closure of the optic fissure, producing a keyhole pupil.
A CHD7-related congenital syndrome: Coloboma, Heart defects, choanal Atresia, Retardation of growth, Genital and Ear anomalies.
Reduced flow in the posterior circulation, causing transient vertigo, diplopia, ataxia, and drop attacks.
Elastic stockings that apply graded pressure to the legs to improve venous return, used in venous insufficiency and DVT prevention.
Involuntary movement of one muscle group accompanying voluntary movement of another, as seen after facial nerve injury.
Bleeding into the spinal epidural space compressing the cord, causing back pain and neurologic deficit; a risk with epidural anesthesia in anticoagulated patients.
A recurrent major depression with a seasonal pattern, usually in winter, treated with bright-light therapy.
An oral nitrate vasodilator that releases nitric oxide, used for angina and heart failure.
Surgical cutting of fascia to relieve pressure in compartment syndrome.
Chronic bladder pain with urgency and frequency without infection, more common in women.
A resin applied topically to treat genital warts (condylomata acuminata). It inhibits microtubules and is not for pregnancy.
A caustic agent used topically to remove genital warts and in chemical peels.
Viral proteins that coat and protect the genome inside the capsid.
A surgical incision into the chest wall, such as emergency left anterolateral thoracotomy in trauma.
Reduced amount of blood pumped by the heart per minute, causing hypotension and hypoperfusion, as in cardiogenic shock.
Tissue injury from acids or alkalis; alkali burns penetrate deeper (liquefactive necrosis), and treatment is copious irrigation.
A topical sulfonamide used on burns, penetrating eschar. It inhibits carbonic anhydrase and may cause metabolic acidosis.
A chemotherapy drug that cross-links DNA after bioreductive activation, used for bladder and anal cancers.
Cancer remaining after surgery or treatment, graded R1 (microscopic) or R2 (macroscopic).
Dangerously high pressure within the abdomen after trauma or surgery, impairing venous return and causing oliguria and organ dysfunction.
Placing a tube through the skin into the renal pelvis to drain obstructed urine.
A hip fracture through the neck of the femur, common in elderly women with osteoporosis, risking avascular necrosis.
Tests measuring the speed and size of electrical signals along nerves, used to diagnose neuropathy and demyelination.
Propagation of action potentials along a nerve; speed rises with myelination and axon diameter.
A break of the forearm bone near the wrist; Colles fracture shows dorsal displacement after falling on an outstretched hand.
A pus-filled liver collection from biliary or portal infection, often polymicrobial including Klebsiella and E. coli.
Imaging using a radioactive tracer (commonly fluorodeoxyglucose) to show metabolic activity, used in cancer staging.
Milky peritoneal fluid rich in triglycerides from lymphatic leakage, due to lymphoma, trauma or cirrhosis.
Incomplete cervical cord injury from hyperextension, causing weakness greater in the arms than legs.
An unstable isotope emitting radiation, used in imaging and therapy.
Opening a narrowed artery by inflating a balloon on a catheter, often followed by stent placement.
Inherited disorders of hemoglobin structure (sickle cell disease) or production (thalassemia).
A seizure disorder of infancy with clusters of flexor spasms and EEG hypsarrhythmia (West syndrome); associated with tuberous sclerosis and treated with ACTH.
Synthetic ACTH used in the stimulation test for adrenal insufficiency.
A technique that shows patients physiologic signals so they learn to control them, used for incontinence and tension headache.
Chronic vulvar pain of at least 3 months without an identifiable cause.
A shallow leg ulcer, often near the medial malleolus, from chronic venous insufficiency.
A skin reaction to a medication, ranging from morbilliform rash to severe forms like Stevens-Johnson syndrome.
An antibody against streptolysin O of group A Streptococcus, whose rising titer shows recent infection, as in rheumatic fever.
Small itchy vesicles or red papules from blocked sweat ducts in hot humid conditions.
Passage of some but not all products of conception, with an open cervix and bleeding.
A hole in the uterine wall, usually from instrumentation such as dilation and curettage or IUD insertion.
The part of the fetus lying over the pelvic inlet (vertex, breech or shoulder). Malpresentation raises the need for cesarean delivery.
Artificial rupture of the amniotic membranes to induce or speed labor.
Transvaginal ultrasound measure of the cervix; a short length predicts preterm birth.
Brain infarction from a clot that travels from elsewhere, commonly the heart in atrial fibrillation, and sudden onset.
An early beat arising from the atria, with an abnormal P wave and usually narrow QRS; usually benign.
Weakness of both legs, as in spinal cord disease.
Gallbladder infection by gas-forming organisms, especially in diabetics, with gas in the wall on imaging.
Septic thrombophlebitis of the internal jugular vein after pharyngitis, caused by Fusobacterium necrophorum, with septic emboli to the lungs.
Treatments such as hemodialysis, peritoneal dialysis, or transplantation that replace failed kidney function.
Surgical exposure of a fracture to realign bone fragments, usually with internal fixation.
Realigning a fracture by manipulation without surgery.
The whipworm, a nematode causing intestinal infection with abdominal pain and, in heavy infection, rectal prolapse.
Nonallergic chronic nasal congestion from autonomic dysregulation triggered by temperature or irritants.
A topical alpha-adrenergic decongestant. Prolonged use causes rebound congestion (rhinitis medicamentosa).
An anaerobic gram-negative rod causing Lemierre syndrome and pharyngitis.
Obligate intracellular fungus-like parasites causing chronic diarrhea in immunocompromised patients.
A high-risk HPV type, with HPV 16, responsible for most cervical cancers via E6 and E7 proteins that inactivate p53 and Rb.
Tuberculous infection of the spine, usually the thoracic vertebrae, causing vertebral collapse and gibbus.
A genus of gram-negative enteric bacilli that cause urinary tract and opportunistic infections.
Proteins in the cell nucleus targeted by autoantibodies in lupus and other autoimmune diseases, as in the antinuclear antibody test.
Congenital absence of skin, typically on the scalp, appearing as an ulcer or scar. Can be seen in trisomy 13.
An antimuscarinic drug used as a patch for motion sickness; it causes dry mouth and sedation.
Drugs that block serotonin receptors. Ondansetron blocks 5-HT3 to prevent nausea.
An H2-receptor blocker for acid reflux, withdrawn from the US market because of NDMA contamination.
The S-isomer of omeprazole, a proton pump inhibitor that reduces gastric acid.
A stool softener that lets water enter the stool.
Hepatitis C drugs ending in -previr that block the viral NS3/4A protease needed to process viral proteins.
A lipid second messenger made from PIP2 by phospholipase C that activates protein kinase C.
The front lobe of the pituitary (adenohypophysis), derived from Rathke pouch, secreting ACTH, TSH, FSH, LH, GH and prolactin.
Releasing and inhibiting hormones made by the hypothalamus that control the pituitary, such as TRH, CRH, GnRH, GHRH and dopamine.
A hormone made by the placenta that maintains the corpus luteum early in pregnancy; it is the basis of pregnancy tests and a tumor marker.
The main protein in milk, which precipitates in acid.
A transporter on thyroid follicular cells that actively takes iodide from blood. It is the basis for radioiodine therapy.
A radioactive technetium-99m ion used in thyroid scans and detection of Meckel diverticulum.
Congenital adrenal hyperplasia with excess androgens, such as 21-hydroxylase deficiency, causing virilization of girls.
Waist circumference divided by hip circumference, a measure of central obesity and cardiovascular risk.
Disorders of the parathyroid glands, such as hyperparathyroidism or hypoparathyroidism, altering calcium levels.
The saddle-shaped depression in the sphenoid bone that houses the pituitary gland.
A pituitary hormone that stimulates growth through IGF-1. Excess causes gigantism or acromegaly.
The ratio of a fluid's density to that of water; urine specific gravity reflects concentrating ability of the kidney.
Ectopic thyroid tissue at the base of the tongue from failed descent of the thyroid.
An HLA class II allele associated with Hashimoto thyroiditis and pernicious anemia.
IgG4-related pancreatic inflammation causing painless jaundice and a sausage-shaped pancreas, responsive to steroids.
Enlarged thyroid with multiple nodules, often from iodine deficiency; may cause hyperthyroidism or compression.
A dye used to detect amyloid, which shows apple-green birefringence under polarized light.
A rash with migrating red patches and blistering in the groin and legs, classically with a glucagonoma.
Drugs that stimulate pancreatic beta cells to release insulin, such as sulfonylureas and meglitinides.
A catecholamine metabolite excreted in urine, elevated in pheochromocytoma and neuroblastoma.
The main metabolite of dopamine, elevated in neuroblastoma.
Paraganglia near the aortic bifurcation, a site of extra-adrenal pheochromocytoma.
A radiolabeled norepinephrine analog used to image and treat pheochromocytoma and neuroblastoma.
Rapid chaotic eye movements with jerking limbs, associated with neuroblastoma in children and autoimmunity.
A peptide similar to gastrin-releasing peptide, expressed by small cell lung cancer.
A rapid-acting insulin analog with quick onset used at mealtime.
Insulin analogs such as lispro, aspart and glulisine that begin working within 15 minutes, used for mealtime coverage.
A long-acting basal insulin analog with a flat, peakless profile lasting about 24 hours.
A first-generation sulfonylurea that stimulates insulin release; may cause disulfiram-like reaction and SIADH.
A first-generation sulfonylurea that closes beta-cell ATP-sensitive potassium channels to increase insulin release.
A second-generation sulfonylurea that closes potassium channels in beta cells, increasing insulin release. Hypoglycemia is the main risk.
A second-generation sulfonylurea that increases insulin secretion and carries hypoglycemia risk.
A GLP-1 receptor agonist injected for type 2 diabetes. It may cause pancreatitis.
A GLP-1 receptor agonist for type 2 diabetes and weight loss. It slows gastric emptying and carries a thyroid C-cell tumor warning.
